patient.chief_complaint: DWI lesion on MRI during a headache with visual aura — diagnosed as migrainous infarction but right eye visual field now has permanent defect
patient.hpi:
A 41-year-old mixed-heritage woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic 6 weeks after an acute hospitalisation. Six weeks ago she presented to the emergency department with a severe headache and left-sided visual disturbance. MRI performed in hospital showed a DWI restriction in the right occipital cortex with corresponding ADC low signal. She was diagnosed with migrainous infarction and started on aspirin 75 mg and sumatriptan was stopped. She has a 12-year history of migraine with visual aura.

The key problem: she has returned because her visual disturbance has NOT resolved — she now has a persistent left homonymous hemianopia that has been present for 6 weeks. She initially assumed this would improve. She underwent formal visual field testing by an optometrist 2 weeks ago who confirmed a 'dense left homonymous hemianopia.'

On careful re-review of the original episode: she had her typical visual aura (expanding shimmering crescent), but the visual loss persisted after the aura should have resolved. The DWI restriction covered the right occipital cortex completely (estimated 3.5cm x 2.5cm). The original MRI report mentioned 'right occipital territorial infarction — posterior cerebral artery territory — causes include migrainous infarction and embolic occlusion.'

She has had 12 years of typical migraine with visual aura; this is the first episode with persistent visual deficit. She is not on the combined OCP (appropriately stopped 12 years ago). She has no hypertension, no AF (she was told by the hospital). BMI 26. Non-smoker.
pmh: Migrainous infarction — 6 weeks ago (diagnosis under review)
No hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease

family_history: Mother has migraine without aura; paternal grandfather had stroke at 70; no family history of AF or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Medical secretary; non-smoker; no alcohol; married; two children (aged 8 and 10); concerned about visual field and return to work

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, fully oriented. Anxious; navigating around left visual field deficit. No cognitive impairment.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Dense left homonymous hemianopia — loss of entire left hemifield bilaterally; macular sparing present (central 5 degrees preserved). PERRLA — direct and consensual reflexes intact bilaterally. Fundoscopy: Normal discs bilaterally. Normal extraocular movements. Visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Sensation intact to light touch and pinprick bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. No Babinski.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait normal — compensates for left visual field deficit.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Cardioembolic right PCA territory ischaemic stroke occurring during a migraine episode — NOT migrainous infarction; paroxysmal AF identified on ILR; switch aspirin to DOAC

differential.key_features: Migrainous infarction: typically small <10mm; within aura territory; all other causes excluded; this case has 3.5cm infarction, complete homonymous hemianopia, PAF found on ILR — migrainous infarction excluded by size and cardioembolic source identified

differential.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with PCA territory stroke
differential.key_features: Initial weakly positive aCL IgG; however, repeat negative at 12 weeks — APS excluded; primary aetiology is PAF

optimal_actions.action: Reconside original migrainous infarction diagnosis — infarct 3.5cm x 2.5cm is too large for migrainous infarction; complete homonymous hemianopia suggests large vessel territory
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Large PCA territorial infarction inconsistent with migrainous infarction; original MRA showed possible right PCA occlusion

optimal_actions.action: Prolonged cardiac monitoring (ILR) — short Holter in hospital insufficient; paroxysmal AF detected on ILR
optimal_actions.expected_finding: PAF detected on ILR — not found on initial Holter

optimal_actions.action: URGENT: Switch aspirin to apixaban 5 mg BID — CHA2DS2-VASc 3 (female + prior stroke); PAF confirmed
optimal_actions.expected_finding: DOAC indicated; aspirin monotherapy insufficient for AF secondary stroke prevention

optimal_actions.action: Repeat antiphospholipid antibodies at 12 weeks — original weakly positive aCL requires confirmation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Repeat negative — APS excluded; transient elevation

optimal_actions.action: Neuro-ophthalmology referral; DVLA notification (homonymous hemianopia = cannot drive)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Complete homonymous hemianopia = DVLA automatic driving revocation; low vision rehab

critical_actions: Revise original migrainous infarction diagnosis — infarct is too large (3.5cm) and complete hemianopia is inconsistent with small migrainous infarction
Paroxysmal AF is the confirmed cardioembolic source — ILR essential for detection when initial Holter was negative
Switch aspirin to DOAC (apixaban) immediately — CHA2DS2-VASc 3 with confirmed PAF and prior stroke; aspirin monotherapy is insufficient
DVLA notification: complete homonymous hemianopia = cannot drive — urgent
Repeat aCL antibodies at 12 weeks — weakly positive result requires confirmation (negative on repeat = APS excluded)
contraindicated_actions: Do not maintain aspirin monotherapy — confirmed PAF with prior stroke requires DOAC
Do not use triptans in future given prior cardioembolic stroke (not migrainous infarction — but caution appropriate)
Do not permit driving — complete homonymous hemianopia = DVLA licence revocation
key_reasoning_points: Large PCA territory infarction (3.5cm x 2.5cm) with complete homonymous hemianopia is inconsistent with typical migrainous infarction (which causes small <10mm cortical lesions)
The original MRA hint of right PCA occlusion was NOT followed up — this was a missed finding indicating proximal embolic PCA occlusion
Paroxysmal AF was only detected on ILR (30 days) not on initial 24-hour Holter — shortduration monitoring is insufficient for post-stroke AF detection
Weakly positive antiphospholipid antibody requires repeat at 12 weeks — initial positive was transient and non-specific; APS definitively excluded on repeat
The patient had a real cardioembolic stroke that coincided with a migraine episode — the migraine aura was a witness to the stroke, not the cause

metadata.condition_name: Cardioembolic PCA stroke (paroxysmal AF) misdiagnosed as migrainous infarction — size criteria, ILR AF detection, DOAC switch
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: established migraineur with DWI restriction is presumed migrainous infarction; large infarct size and complete hemianopia should raise suspicion; ILR detects PAF missed on initial Holter; DOAC urgently needed

results.title: ICHD-3 Migrainous Infarction: Diagnostic Criteria and Imaging
results.authors: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS.
results.summary: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.1) typically causes small (<10mm) cortical or juxtacortical lesions strictly within the aura territory; full homonymous hemianopia is UNUSUAL in true migrainous infarction; all other causes must be excluded before diagnosing migrainous infarction.

results.title: Cardioembolic vs Migrainous PCA Territory Stroke: Distinguishing Features
results.summary: Large territorial PCA infarctions (>2cm) causing complete homonymous hemianopia are inconsistent with migrainous infarction; complete hemianopia suggests proximal PCA embolism from cardioembolic source; original MRA showing possible PCA occlusion is a key differentiating finding.

results.title: Paroxysmal AF Detection After Cryptogenic Stroke — ILR vs Short Holter
results.summary: 30-day ILR detects paroxysmal AF in 12-15% of cryptogenic stroke patients vs <3% with 24-hour Holter; PAF is confirmed as cardioembolic source; DOAC anticoagulation provides secondary stroke prevention superior to aspirin alone.

output.summary: ICHD-3 migrainous infarction typically causes small lesions (<10mm) strictly within the aura territory; large territorial infarctions with complete homonymous hemianopia are inconsistent with migrainous infarction and suggest proximal embolic PCA occlusion. Short-duration Holter monitoring detects AF in fewer than 3% of cryptogenic stroke patients; 30-day ILR detection rate is approximately 12-15%. Confirmed AF is managed with DOAC anticoagulation for secondary stroke prevention.

output.proposed: apixaban 5 mg BID replacing aspirin 75 mg; PAF secondary stroke prevention
warnings: Concurrent aspirin + DOAC increases bleeding risk without additional embolic stroke prevention benefit compared to DOAC monotherapy — dual therapy should generally be avoided
DOAC anticoagulation is indicated in atrial fibrillation with elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score (≥2 in women, ≥1 in men); female sex and prior stroke each contribute independently to CHA2DS2-VASc scoring

output.query: rehabilitation persistent homonymous hemianopia post-stroke visual field recovery DVLA driving

results.title: Visual Recovery After Occipital Stroke and Homonymous Hemianopia
results.summary: Spontaneous recovery from homonymous hemianopia occurs in ~40% within 3 months post-stroke; macular sparing is commonly preserved due to dual MCA-PCA blood supply to the macular cortex; visual compensation therapy involving eye movement training into the blind field improves functional disability.

results.title: Prism Therapy and Visual Rehabilitation for Hemianopia
results.summary: Sector prisms (Fresnel prisms) can expand effective visual field awareness; formal low vision rehabilitation including compensatory saccade training improves daily function; occupational therapy for work adaptation recommended for patients in visual detail-dependent roles.

results.title: DVLA Driving Regulations and Visual Field Defects
results.summary: Complete homonymous hemianopia = automatic DVLA Category I driving licence revocation; patients must not drive until assessed and cleared by DVLA; formal notification required; neuro-ophthalmology assessment for DVLA medical review pathway.

output.summary: Post-stroke homonymous hemianopia is managed with neuro-ophthalmology review and low vision rehabilitation including compensatory saccade training; complete homonymous hemianopia triggers automatic DVLA Category I licence revocation pending formal neuro-ophthalmology assessment; occupational therapy supports work adaptation in visually-demanding roles. Clinical correlation recommended.
